# SK3001 — `async void` outside an event handler

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An `async void` method that nothing subscribes as an event handler.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | none |
| Scope | Compilation |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 0.8 |

## Why

An `async void` method cannot be awaited, so its caller cannot know when it finished and cannot observe its exceptions. An exception thrown after the first `await` is raised on whatever synchronization context resumed the method, which in a console or server process means an unhandled exception that terminates it. `async Task` gives the caller both. The one legitimate use is an event handler, whose delegate type returns `void` and whose exceptions the framework expects to handle, so the rule is silent there.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
async void SaveAsync() {
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(path, text);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
async Task SaveAsync() {
    await File.WriteAllTextAsync(path, text);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The rule ships disabled — `defaultSeverity: none` — and this is the interesting part of its story rather than a hedge.** It is silent on anything that could be an event handler or is bound to a delegate: an `override`, a `virtual` or `new` method (whose return type binds every override below it), any method implementing an interface member, any method whose name begins `On`, any method with the `(object, EventArgs)` shape, any method carrying an attribute, a partial method, and — the check that costs the most — every method whose name appears anywhere in the compilation in a position other than a direct invocation, which covers `+=` subscription, a method group passed as an argument and a delegate construction. That last check is why the rule is compilation-scoped and can never be served from the per-file incremental cache.

⚠ **One measurement decides the default, and it is not a finding count.** M6 stacked two reasons and docs/plan/16 § "The reference trees are a test subject" struck one of them: "the rule fires zero times on both reference trees" is a fact about those trees, never a reason to disable a rule that is right. What survives is the cost. A compilation-scoped rule's answer for one file depends on files that file's cache key does not name, so enabling it sends every run with a change down the cold path — measured at M9 over Skala's own tree with `skala check --profile`, **8.5 s against a warm 6.9 s**, with the analyzer phase going from a single tree to all of them. Charging that to every repository for a rule whose benefit is unmeasured is the trade docs/plan/08 § "Reasons that justify a cut" calls reason 2, so the rule ships off and a repository that has `async void` turns it on deliberately.

⚠ **Turning it on no longer costs the warm path, and it no longer needs `--no-cache` (#364).** Until 2026-09-11 `IncrementalAnalysis` decided whether the warm path was available by reading `descriptor.IsEnabledByDefault`, which comes from this file and which an `.editorconfig` severity does not change, so an opted-in repository kept the warm path while the cache dropped this rule's findings for every unchanged file. The incremental pass now partitions analyzers by scope instead: this rule's analyzer is in the whole-compilation bucket whether it is on or off, re-runs over the whole compilation on every warm run while the per-file entries keep serving, and Roslyn skips it while it is off. The 8.5 s against 6.9 s above was the price of the old guard sending *everything* cold; the price now is this analyzer alone over the compilation. docs/plan/16 § "The opt-in that does not cost what it says" is the record.

## Configuration

- `dotnet_diagnostic.SK3001.severity (`none` by default; set it to `warning` to enable — the rule is compilation-scoped, so once on it re-runs over the whole compilation on every warm run beside the per-file cache rather than through it; the per-file entries keep serving and nothing else is needed, #364)`
